new.title: Go underground in Europe's termite mound
new.desc: Beneath the citadel runs one of the longest networks of military tunnels on the continent. The guided tour leads you through about half a kilometre of cool, damp galleries with light and sound effects that bring the sieges back to life.
new.tip: Tours leave from the Terra Nova visitor centre and need booking; bring a jumper, as it stays around 12 to 14 degrees down there and there are 350 steps.
new.q: Terra Nova Citadelle de Namur

new.title: Float up to the citadel by téléphérique
new.desc: Namur's cable car reopened in 2021, a quarter century after the old 1956 line shut down, and lifts you from the Sambre quay to the citadel esplanade in under seven minutes, with the rooftops and both rivers sliding away beneath you.
new.tip: Ride up and walk down through the woods and ramparts; the old Belvédère station of the first cable car is still visible on the hill.
new.q: Téléphérique de Namur Place Maurice Servais

new.title: Blush a little at the Musée Félicien Rops
new.desc: Namur's native son Félicien Rops was a caricaturist, engraver and provocateur of 19th-century symbolism. His family's townhouse now holds the world's largest collection of his work, from biting cartoons to the scandalous Pornocratès.
new.tip: Don't skip the small garden, replanted around Rops' love of botany. Entry is free on the first Sunday of the month.
new.q: Musée Félicien Rops Rue Fumal 12 Namur

new.title: Find Don Juan's heart in Saint-Aubain cathedral
new.desc: Namur's cathedral is an 18th-century Baroque and neoclassical temple by the Italian architect Pisoni, crowned by a dome about 70 metres high. Behind the high altar a niche keeps the heart of Don Juan of Austria, victor of Lepanto, who died near Namur.
new.tip: The nave is open outside services; the square in front is where the stilt fighters clash during the Fêtes de Wallonie.
new.q: Cathédrale Saint-Aubain Namur

new.title: Spot the UNESCO belfry hiding in plain sight
new.desc: The Tour Saint-Jacques was built in 1388 as part of the city walls and only became Namur's belfry in 1746, after the old clock church burned in a siege. It is the oldest of the three surviving medieval wall towers and part of the UNESCO list of belfries.
new.tip: Look up at the octagonal top that encloses the clock, then wander on to Place d'Armes and Rue de Fer, a few steps away.
new.q: Beffroi de Namur Rue du Beffroi

new.title: Marvel at the Treasure of Oignies at TreM.a
new.desc: Brother Hugo d'Oignies was one of the great Mosan goldsmiths of the 13th century, and his reliquaries, crosses and book covers, glittering with filigree and gems, are counted among the wonders of Belgium. They are shown at TreM.a, the museum of ancient art in a mansion on Rue de Fer.
new.tip: Combine it with the rest of TreM.a's medieval and Renaissance collection; like the Rops museum it joins the free first Sunday of the month.
new.q: TreM.a Musée des Arts anciens Rue de Fer 24 Namur

new.title: Sit on the Grognon steps where Sambre meets Meuse
new.desc: The tip of land at the foot of the citadel, the old Grognon, has been redesigned as the Espace Confluence: broad stone steps that run down to the water right where the two rivers merge, facing the Walloon Parliament.
new.tip: Come at sunset with a drink from the brasserie at Le NID and watch the boats turn in from both rivers.
new.q: Place du Grognon Namur

new.title: Cross L'Enjambée to Jambes
new.desc: Opened in 2020, this footbridge and cycle bridge leaps the Meuse from the confluence to Jambes. Its see-through lattice railings mean the best view of the Grognon, the old Saint-Gilles hospice and the citadel is from the middle of the river.
new.tip: On the Jambes side, treat yourself at the Glacetronome artisan ice cream shop and look back at the old town.
new.q: Passerelle L'Enjambée Namur Jambes

new.title: Catch the citadel view from the roof of Le Delta
new.desc: The province's cultural centre on the Sambre quay has a panoramic rooftop terrace that locals rate as one of the best spots to see the citadel from the lower town.
new.tip: Exhibitions are often free, so you can go up without a show ticket; browse local crafts at the Fait Main shop in the rotunda on the way.
new.q: Le Delta Avenue Fernand Golenvaux 18 Namur

new.title: Hop across the river on a Namourette
new.desc: These little retro whaleboats ferry people from bank to bank of the Sambre and the Meuse, a cheap and charming way to see Namur from water level.
new.tip: They sail daily in July and August and at weekends in May, June and September; one of the stops is at the foot of Le Delta, and children ride free.
new.q: Namourettes Namur Le Delta

new.title: Raise a péket at Le Ratin-Tôt
new.desc: On the lively Place du Marché aux Légumes, Le Ratin-Tôt is said to be the oldest café still pouring in Namur. It is the place to try péket, the Walloon juniper spirit that flows freely in this town.
new.tip: Grab a seat on the square's terrace on a sunny afternoon; the little bars of Rue Lelièvre near the cathedral are next on a local pub crawl.
new.q: Le Ratin-Tôt Place du Marché aux Légumes Namur

new.title: Order cassolette namuroise on Rue des Brasseurs
new.desc: Namur's signature casserole of veal and kidney with rice, flamed with péket, is a fixture at Le Temps des Cerises, a snug red-and-white bistro in the old town whose walls are covered in signatures of famous guests. Escargots à la namuroise are on the menu too.
new.tip: Book ahead, especially if you want one of the little rooms upstairs; Rue des Brasseurs is Namur's main going-out street, so stay for a drink afterwards.
new.q: Le Temps des Cerises Rue des Brasseurs 22 Namur

new.title: Shop the Saturday market by the Sambre
new.desc: Namur's main weekly market has moved to the water's edge along the Sambre and Boulevard Frère Orban, with the citadel as a backdrop. Locals come for regional cheese, charcuterie, fruit and vegetables.
new.tip: Go early in the morning, as it winds down around lunchtime; in early summer look for Wépion strawberries.
new.q: Marché du Bord de l'Eau Boulevard Frère Orban Namur

new.title: Taste Namur's own beers at the citadel
new.desc: Namur has a lively crop of microbreweries, from Houppe to Vulpio in Wépion, and the citadel celebrates them with a Salon des Bières Namuroises in November. Year-round, the self-service bistro Made in Namur up on the citadel pours local beers, rum and gin.
new.tip: Ask for a Houppe, the amber triple brewed by five Namur friends since 2013, and drink it with the view over the rivers.
new.q: Made in Namur Citadelle de Namur

new.title: Eat Wépion strawberries where they grow
new.desc: Wépion, on the Meuse just south of Namur, is Belgium's strawberry capital. The Musée de la Fraise tells the story of the crop, and the city-run Jardin des Petits Fruits beside it grows some 15 strawberry varieties and many other local berries.
new.tip: The garden is free; buy a punnet from a roadside grower on the Chaussée de Dinant in season, or pick up strawberry liqueur and jam to take home.
new.q: Musée de la Fraise Chaussée de Dinant 1037 Wépion

new.title: Walk the Meuse at Profondeville facing the Rochers de Frênes
new.desc: Across the river from Profondeville, the limestone cliffs of Frênes rise straight out of a bend of the Meuse. The riverside path on the Profondeville bank gives what walkers call the finest view of the rocks.
new.tip: An easy 6 km loop from Profondeville follows the bank and forest paths; it's a short bus or bike ride along the RAVeL from Namur.
new.q: Point de vue Rochers de Frênes Profondeville

new.title: Have cheese and bread at Maredsous Abbey
new.desc: The Benedictine abbey of Maredsous, in a green valley near Denée, draws hundreds of thousands of visitors a year. Its Centre Saint-Joseph has a bakery and a restaurant serving the abbey cheese, partly ripened in the monastery's own cellars, with Maredsous beer.
new.tip: Order the classic plank of Maredsous cheese and abbey bread with a blonde or brune, then walk down into the Molignée valley. Bus 21 runs from Namur station.
new.q: Centre Saint-Joseph Abbaye de Maredsous Denée

new.title: Sip local brews at the Brasserie de la Lesse near Rochefort
new.desc: Rochefort's famous Trappist is brewed behind closed doors at the abbey of Saint-Rémy, but in the village of Eprave the artisanal Brasserie de la Lesse throws its doors open, with a rustic bar and terrace for tasting its own beers.
new.tip: Pair it with the Grotte de Lorette in Rochefort; order a Rochefort 10, one of the strongest Trappists, in any café in town to complete the set.
new.q: Brasserie de la Lesse Rue du Treux 4 Eprave

new.title: Descend into the Grottes de Hotton
new.desc: Discovered by quarrymen in 1958, the 'caves of the 1001 Nights' near Hotton glitter with colourful stalactites, draperies and rimstone pools, and end at a balcony above a gallery about 200 metres long, said to be the largest in Belgium.
new.tip: The guided tour goes down 580 steps, but a lift brings you most of the way back up; it stays around 12 degrees inside. Durbuy is a 15-minute drive away.
new.q: Grottes de Hotton Chemin du Spéléo Club 1

new.title: Read the carved stalls of Saint-Hubert basilica
new.desc: The patron saint of hunters gave his name to this Ardennes town, and the Gothic abbey church that grew around his relics is a minor basilica. Its oak choir stalls from 1733 tell the lives of Saint Benedict and Saint Hubert in eighteen reliefs.
new.tip: On the summer solstice the rising sun lights up the panel of Hubert's conversion; also look for the 19th-century cenotaph King Leopold I commissioned.
new.q: Basilique Saint-Hubert Saint-Hubert

new.title: Step into rural Wallonia at the Fourneau Saint-Michel
new.desc: In the wooded Masblette valley near Saint-Hubert, more than fifty old farms, a chapel, a school and craft workshops from all over Wallonia have been rebuilt as an open-air village. It grew up around an 18th-century iron furnace that belonged to the abbey of Saint-Hubert.
new.tip: Allow half a day; the iron museum by the old furnace is on the same site, and the 'village' is best on a dry day for strolling between the houses.
new.q: Fourneau Saint-Michel Saint-Hubert

new.title: Look down on Frahan from Rochehaut
new.desc: From the roadside viewpoint in Rochehaut, the Semois curls so tightly around the hamlet of Frahan that it almost becomes an island, with wooded ridges, old slate quarries and tobacco dryers all around.
new.tip: Walk down the marked trail to the valley and cross the footbridge to Frahan, then climb back up; Bouillon and the Tombeau du Géant are close by.
new.q: Point de vue de Frahan Rochehaut

new.title: Drift down the Semois by flat boat from Chiny
new.desc: For about a century, ferrymen have poled flat-bottomed boats down the 8 km stretch of the Semois from Chiny to Lacuisine, telling legends about the rocks and banks along the way. It is the gentle alternative to a kayak.
new.tip: Walk back the 4 km through the Chiny forest on the yellow trail, past the Rocher du Hât viewpoint; there is a riverside beach and picnic spot by the Pont Saint-Nicolas.
new.q: Pont Saint-Nicolas Chiny

new.title: Hear the cicadas in Torgny, Belgium's southernmost village
new.desc: Torgny, in the Gaume on the French border, is Belgium's southernmost village and one of the most beautiful in Wallonia. Its warm limestone slopes carry vineyards replanted in 1954 and a nature reserve where cicadas sing, a rarity in Belgium.
new.tip: Walk the trail through the Raymond Mayné nature reserve on a hot summer day to hear the cicadas, then taste the local white wine in the village.
new.q: Torgny Rouvroy

fix.problem: The tip sends people to the 'golden turtle statue' without context. It is Jan Fabre's 'Searching for Utopia'; after Fabre's 2022 conviction the city added a sign stating its disapproval. The tip also says to take the cable car, which is now covered by its own quest.
fix.suggestion: Name the artwork neutrally (Jan Fabre's golden tortoise, 'Searching for Utopia', on the Terra Nova esplanade) or drop it, and point the tip to the ramparts/Terra Nova instead of the cable car.
